title: Camp 2 close: the story you're in
hookLine: parables, a birth, a road, a cross, an empty tomb, a church on the move

lines: A TROUGH, A CROSS, A GARDEN.
A FIRE, A FLAME, A SHIPWRECK.
cards: Seventy-five days of stories. A farmer sowing on every kind of ground. A woman sweeping the house for one coin.
A servant who buried his talent because he was afraid. A young woman in Nazareth saying, let it be. A feeding trough.
Shepherds on the night shift. Fishermen told to put out into the deep. A short man up a tree.
A king on a donkey. A towel and a basin. A rooster.

teach.b: Mark's Gospel, the shortest, begins, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning. Gospel is the old English godspel, good news, translating the Greek euangelion.
The Gospels tell it as a story, not a list of ideas: parables that turn things upside down, a birth in the wrong place, a road through Galilee, one last week in Jerusalem, a cross, and an empty tomb.
And the book of Acts, where this camp has lived for weeks, doesn't end.
Its last scene: Paul under house arrest in Rome two whole years, welcoming all who came, teaching, in the King James words, "with all confidence, no man forbidding him." Then Luke stops.
Acts never tells Paul's trial or his death.
Some readers take that open ending as deliberate: the story keeps going. Through Stephen and Philip and Lydia, then Monica and Augustine, Francis, Teresa, Joan, and names nobody wrote down.
Christians say every life that takes it up becomes another page. That doesn't mean anyone here has to believe it.
Some of you walk this path because it's your faith, some because it's someone else's you love, some just to understand. You've walked its length now, from the sower to the shipwreck.
Next, this path moves from stories to practices: how Christians pray, sing, rest and live it, day to day. Camp three begins tomorrow.

how: Christians retell these stories every year through the church calendar, from the annunciation and Christmas through Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, and remember the saints on their feast days. Many churches read the Gospels and Acts in order across the year.

o: a rule for how a church is run
a preacher sent out to spread the faith
good news, the word behind gospel

s: the book of Acts ends with Paul's death
it ends with Paul teaching in Rome under house arrest, no man forbidding him. the story is left open.
the word gospel comes from the old English for good news
Mark's Gospel begins with the birth of Jesus
it begins: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and goes straight to a man by a river.

games.q: you're Luke, finishing Acts. Paul is in Rome under house arrest, teaching everyone who comes. how do you end the book?
o: with a summary of everything he taught.
mid-story: Paul teaching, no man forbidding him.
games.why: Luke stops with Paul teaching with all confidence, no man forbidding him. some readers take the open ending as deliberate: the story keeps going.

practice: Take the first story from this camp that comes to mind, and ask where it touches your life: the lost coin, the one up the tree, the road to Emmaus, sad, not recognizing something beside you.
Find one sentence that says it, and write it down if you can; if you pray, offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Euangelion. Greek for good news; old English godspel, gospel. Parable, leaven, talent, annunciation, Magnificat, manger, baptism, disciple, the keys, transfiguration, hosanna, Pentecost, martyr, conversion, Gentile, epistle, agape, saint.

orig.note: Greek: good news. The old English godspel, gospel, translates it.
